extracted.intended_audience: general readers of Montaigne; students of Renaissance literature and moral philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading of a Montaigne essay that offers normative guidance on eating, pleasure, temperance, and how to live; the page presents many practical and ethical maxims about conduct and taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aid those most in need rather than those who can benefit you
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer to regard and assist those who most need our assistance, rather than those who can do us good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne contrasts Flaminius (who aided the needy) with Pyrrhus (who truckled to the great); examples include Cheilonis and choices in wartime. Implied anti-pattern: favoring the powerful for reciprocal advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclination toward the meaner sort; humility toward fortune
rubrics_metrics.description: Have an inclination toward the meaner sort of people and prefer moderate, humble company over flourishing, successful factions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne explains this is partly from natural compassion and partly from a desire to cleave to those in need; the preference functions as a moral stance and social orientation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer moderate, deliberate dining and conversational accompaniment
rubrics_metrics.description: Eat deliberately and intermix eating with profitable conversation; treat eating as a principal action of life deserving leisure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ancients set long hours for eating to extend pleasure and useful talk. Varro’s requirements for good entertainments are cited: graceful persons, agreeable conversation (neither silent nor garrulous), neatness and delicacy of meat and place, and fair weather.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid long sittings and speaking on a full stomach
rubrics_metrics.description: Long sittings at table both trouble and harm; speaking on a full stomach tires and hurts one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne sits shortly at his own house and likes to listen rather than talk after a meal; imitates Augustus in timing but not in rising early. Anti-pattern: prolonged feasting that impairs health or conversation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control temptation when fasting by avoiding exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: When fasting, remove oneself from suppers and be kept apart from tempting food; resolve requires controlling the environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne notes that if a fasted dish comes into sight, persuasion to forbear is in vain. Practical guidance: arrange family and servants to enforce a prescribed collation and keep tempting foods out of sight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperance seasons pleasure; avoid intemperance
rubrics_metrics.description: Intemperance is the pest of pleasure; temperance is not its scourge but its seasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne cites Euxodus and others who tasted sovereign good through moderation. Practical rule: enjoy pleasures with moderation so they remain sweet and sustainable; anti-pattern: habitual excess that destroys future liberty to vary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value bodily pleasures as natural and legitimate
rubrics_metrics.description: Bodily pleasures are natural, not brutish, and should not be despised by the wise; they are to be enjoyed in measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne criticizes philosophies that wholly reject the body (Pythagoras) or wholly prioritize it (Aristippus), advocating a balanced view (Socratic/Platonic mean). Anti-pattern: moralizing contempt for natural pleasures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek a balance between contemplation and action
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid extremes of pure contemplation or pure sensualism; adopt a mean between the two and let each part (mind/body) aid the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne praises Socrates as exemplifying this balance; recommendation: when dancing, dance; when sleeping, sleep — be fully present but not exclusively so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Savor and ruminate on present pleasures to deepen their value
rubrics_metrics.description: When experiencing a good state, do not merely let it pass: taste it over again, adhere to it, ruminate upon it, and bring the soul to partake of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne describes deliberately disturbing sleep to better relish it and using reason to amplify present contentment; practical technique for increasing the 'weight' of short life by deeper enjoyment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live purposefully: make life fuller rather than merely longer
rubrics_metrics.description: The glorious masterpiece of man is to live to purpose; other achievements are appendices to living well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given brevity of life, extend its weight by vigorous use and purposeful conduct. Anti-pattern: chasing length of life or external achievements over the art of living itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greatness of soul is self-government and choosing the moderate
rubrics_metrics.description: True greatness consists in knowing how to govern and circumscribe oneself; prefer moderate things that are enough rather than eminent excesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne argues moderation demonstrates greatness; practical application: exercise restraint and prefer sufficiency over ostentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid escalation of comforts and superstitious accretions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not habitually add layers of comfort (clothing, accessories) that lead to endless gradation and dependence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne warns how a small accommodation (coif to kerchief to cap to quilted hat) becomes a slippery slope. Rule: resist progressive accoutrement and return to simpler habits when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe and practice civil table manners: do not eat greedily
rubrics_metrics.description: Eating greedily is indecent and harms both health and the pleasure of the table; one should chew with grace and allow leisure for discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdotes: Diogenes boxed a tutor for permitting a boy to eat greedily; Romans taught graceful chewing. Practical: eat at a pace that allows conversation and savoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fortitude must oppose both pain and immoderate pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Fortitude is equally the office to fight against pain and against the charming blandishments of pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cicero and Plato invoked: take pain medicinally and scantily, take pleasure as needed but not to drunkenness. Practical approach: regulate indulgence as one would tolerate necessary suffering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature ordains that necessary actions be pleasurable; do not divorce necessity from delight
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature has observed that actions necessary to life should also be pleasurable; it is unjust to separate the divine/intellectual from the earthly/physical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne suggests confirming the union of mind and body by mutual offices: let mind quicken body and body steady soul. Anti-pattern: ascetic denial that treats natural pleasures as inherently base.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participate in simple communal pleasures; relaxation honors the strong soul
rubrics_metrics.description: Taking part heartily in songs, sports, dances, and simple amusements does not detract from honor or virtue; relaxation and facility become a generous soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Epaminondas and Scipio enjoying childish amusements; Socrates learning dancing and playing instruments. Practical: include communal, physical pleasures as part of a balanced life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept natural aging and death with calm; do not fear what follows natural course
rubrics_metrics.description: Death that comes by old age is natural and the least violent; accept the gradual decline and find consolation in its just and natural progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne reflects on bodily decay (teeth, sight, hearing) and counsels that what comes according to nature should always be pleasant; anti-pattern: imagining immeasurable and prodigious old age as desirable beyond natural bounds.
